{{Short description|Generalization of the Gaussian measure using the Besov norm}}
{{no footnotes|date=November 2015}}

In [[mathematics]] &mdash; specifically, in the fields of [[probability theory]] and [[inverse problem]]s &mdash; '''Besov measures''' and associated '''Besov-distributed random variables''' are generalisations of the notions of [[Gaussian measure]]s and [[random variables]], [[Laplace distribution]]s, and other classical distributions.  They are particularly useful in the study of [[Bayesian inference|inverse problems]] on [[function space]]s for which a Gaussian [[prior probability|Bayesian prior]] is an inappropriate model.  The construction of a Besov measure is similar to the construction of a [[Besov space]], hence the nomenclature.

== Definitions ==

Let <math>H</math> be a [[separable space|separable]] [[Hilbert space]] of functions defined on a domain <math>D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d}</math>, and let <math>\{ e_{n} \mid n \in \mathbb{N} \}</math> be a [[complete orthonormal basis]] for <math>H</math>.  Let <math>s \in \mathbb{R}</math> and <math>1 \leq p < \infty</math>.  For <math>u = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{N}} u_{n} e_{n} \in H</math>, define
:<math>\| u \|_{X^{s, p}} = \left\| \sum_{n \in \mathbb{N}} u_{n} e_{n} \right\|_{X^{s,p}} := \left( \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} n^{( \frac{p s}{d} + \frac{p}{2} - 1)} | u_{n} |^{p} \right)^{1/p}.</math>
This defines a [[norm (mathematics)|norm]] on the subspace of <math>H</math> for which it is finite, and we let <math>X^{s, p}</math> denote the [[Complete metric space#Completion|completion]] of this subspace with respect to this new norm.  The motivation for these definitions arises from the fact that <math>\| u \|_{X^{s, p}}</math> is equivalent to the norm of <math>u</math> in the Besov space <math>B_{p p}^{s}(D)</math>.

Let <math>\kappa > 0</math> be a scale parameter, similar to the precision (the reciprocal of the [[variance]]) of a Gaussian measure.  We now define a <math>X^{s, p}</math>-valued random variable <math>u</math> by
:<math>u := \sum_{n \in \mathbb{N}} n^{-(\frac{s}{d} + \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{p})} \kappa^{- \frac{1}{p}} \xi_{n} e_{n},</math>
where <math>\xi_{1}, \xi_{2}, \dots</math> are sampled independently and identically from the generalized Gaussian measure on <math>\mathbb{R}</math> with Lebesgue [[probability density function]] proportional to <math>\exp ( - \tfrac{1}{2} | \xi_{n} |^{p} )</math>.  Informally, <math>u</math> can be said to have a probability density function proportional to <math>\exp (- \tfrac{\kappa}{2} \| u \|_{X^{s, p}}^{p} )</math> with respect to infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure ([[Infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure|which does not make rigorous sense]]), and is therefore a natural candidate for a "typical" element of <math>X^{s, p}</math> (although this Is not quite true &mdash; see below).

==Properties==

It is easy to show that, when ''t''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''s'', the ''X''<sup>''t'',''p''</sup> norm is finite whenever the ''X''<sup>''s'',''p''</sup> norm is.  Therefore, the spaces ''X''<sup>''s'',''p''</sup> and ''X''<sup>''t'',''p''</sup> are nested:
:<math>X^{s, p} \subseteq X^{t, p} \mbox{ when } t \leq s.</math>
This is consistent with the usual nesting of smoothness classes of functions ''f'':&nbsp;''D''&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''':
for example, the [[Sobolev space]] ''H''<sup>2</sup>(''D'') is a subspace of ''H''<sup>1</sup>(''D'') and in turn of the [[Lp space|Lebesgue space]] ''L''<sup>2</sup>(''D'') = ''H''<sup>0</sup>(''D''); the [[Hölder space]] ''C''<sup>1</sup>(''D'') of continuously differentiable functions is a subspace of the space ''C''<sup>0</sup>(''D'') of continuous functions.

It can be shown that the series defining ''u'' converges in ''X''<sup>''t'',''p''</sup> [[almost surely]] for any ''t''&nbsp;&lt;&nbsp;''s''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''d''&nbsp;/&nbsp;''p'', and therefore gives a well-defined ''X''<sup>''t'',''p''</sup>-valued random variable. Note that ''X''<sup>''t'',''p''</sup> is a larger space than ''X''<sup>''s'',''p''</sup>, and in fact thee random variable ''u'' is [[almost surely]] ''not'' in the smaller space ''X''<sup>''s'',''p''</sup>. The space ''X''<sup>''s'',''p''</sup> is rather the Cameron-Martin space of this probability measure in the Gaussian case ''p''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2. The random variable ''u'' is said to be '''Besov distributed''' with parameters (''&kappa;'', ''s'', ''p''), and the induced [[probability measure]] is called a '''Besov measure'''.
